security_audit.summary: All 81 static findings are false positives caused by Markdown syntax, graph terminology, fixed local I/O examples, and documentation links. The audit found one high-severity issue: the pickle example deserializes a file without warning that untrusted data can execute arbitrary code.

remediation.suggestion: Warn users never to load untrusted pickle files. Prefer GraphML, JSON, or another non-executable format for exchanged data.

content.value_statement: Complex graph data is difficult to model, inspect, and explain. This skill guides NetworkX workflows for construction, analysis, visualization, and export.
actual_capabilities: Build directed, undirected, and multigraph structures with node and edge attributes.
Compute shortest paths, centrality, clustering, connectivity, communities, flows, matching, and traversal results.
Generate classic, random, lattice, tree, bipartite, and domain-specific synthetic networks.
Import and export common graph formats, matrices, tables, and local databases.
Create static and interactive network visualizations with documented layout and styling options.
Select formats, seeds, and approximate algorithms for reproducible large-graph workflows.
limitations: NetworkX stores graphs in memory, so very large networks may require another graph engine.
Optional visualization, matrix, database, and Graphviz workflows require separate dependencies.
Algorithm results depend on graph direction, weights, connectivity, and input quality.
Pickle input is unsafe when files come from untrusted sources.

use_cases.title: Explore relationship data
use_cases.description: Transform tabular relationships into graphs, measure structure, rank important nodes, and explain patterns.

use_cases.title: Model network behavior
use_cases.description: Generate reproducible synthetic networks and compare their topology with observed systems.

use_cases.title: Build graph workflows
use_cases.description: Choose graph types, algorithms, file formats, and visual outputs for Python applications.

prompt_templates.title: Summarize an edge list
prompt_templates.prompt: Create an undirected NetworkX graph from this edge list: {edges}. Report node count, edge count, density, connected components, and assumptions.
prompt_templates.scenario: Begin with a small unweighted relationship dataset.

prompt_templates.title: Rank influential nodes
prompt_templates.prompt: Analyze this weighted directed graph: {data}. Identify influential nodes using three suitable centrality measures. Explain why each measure fits.
prompt_templates.scenario: Compare influence measures for a directed network.

prompt_templates.title: Evaluate communities
prompt_templates.prompt: Compare suitable NetworkX community detection methods for this network: {data}. Recommend one method, set reproducible parameters, and explain evaluation criteria.
prompt_templates.scenario: Select a defensible community detection workflow.

prompt_templates.title: Design a graph pipeline
prompt_templates.prompt: Design a memory-aware NetworkX pipeline for {dataset}. Validate identifiers and weights. Analyze paths and communities. Export interoperable results and a publication-ready visualization.
prompt_templates.scenario: Plan an advanced workflow from ingestion through reporting.

output_examples.input: Analyze an undirected collaboration network with 240 nodes and 612 edges.
output: Summary: 240 nodes, 612 edges, density 0.021, and 3 connected components.
Key result: the largest component contains 92 percent of nodes.
Recommendation: inspect component boundaries before comparing centrality scores.

output_examples.input: Plan a reproducible comparison of small-world and scale-free networks with 1,000 nodes.
output: Method: generate both models with fixed seeds and comparable mean degree.
Compare degree distribution, clustering, average path length, and component structure.
Report parameter choices and uncertainty across repeated runs.

output_examples.input: Choose a format that preserves graph attributes across Python and Gephi.
output_examples.output: Recommendation: use GraphML because it preserves attributes and works across common graph tools. Validate attribute types before export.

best_practices: Confirm graph type, edge direction, weight meaning, and node identifiers before selecting algorithms.
Set random seeds and record model parameters for reproducible generation and layouts.
Validate on a small sample before running expensive metrics on the full graph.
anti_patterns: Do not apply connected-graph algorithms without checking components and direction.
Do not interpret centrality rankings without considering graph construction and missing relationships.
Do not deserialize pickle files from unknown or untrusted sources.

faq.question: Which NetworkX versions does this skill support?
faq.answer: It provides general API guidance, but the installed version controls exact availability. Check official documentation for version-specific behavior.

faq.question: Can it analyze directed and weighted graphs?
faq.answer: Yes. Specify edge direction, weight meaning, and the algorithms that should use weights.

faq.question: Is NetworkX suitable for very large graphs?
faq.answer: NetworkX is memory based. Large workloads may need sampling, approximate methods, sparse matrices, or a specialized graph engine.

faq.question: Which graph formats are covered?
faq.answer: The references cover edge lists, GraphML, GML, JSON, CSV, matrices, compressed files, SQLite, DOT, and several specialized formats.

faq.question: Can it create network visualizations?
faq.answer: Yes. It covers NetworkX layouts, Matplotlib styling, interactive libraries, three-dimensional views, and publication-ready exports.

faq.question: How should untrusted graph files be handled?
faq.answer: Prefer non-executable formats and validate content before parsing. Never load an untrusted pickle file.
